name: SketchUp
tagline: Push-pull 3D modeling for architecture, woodworking, and anyone who wants to draw a building without learning Revit.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: An agent can absolutely give you a three.js scene where you draw a rectangle and pull it into a box, and that demo will feel great for about ten minutes. Then you try to cut a window into a wall, union two solids, soften an edge, or import a DWG, and you discover that the hard part of SketchUp was never the UI. It is the geometry kernel, the inference engine that guesses which edge you meant to snap to, and twenty years of handling degenerate meshes without exploding. Add the 3D Warehouse full of pre-modeled sinks and sofas, the Ruby extension ecosystem, and LayOut for turning a model into printable drawings, and the surface area gets silly. The honest consolation build is a toy push-pull modeler, useful for learning, not for your kitchen remodel.
coreLoopDIY: A browser app where you draw 2D polygons on a grid plane, extrude them into solids with a drag, orbit the camera, and export the result as GLTF or STL.
requirements: Comfort with three.js and basic computational geometry
No accounts, no cloud, runs entirely local
whatYouLose: A real solid modeling kernel: booleans, clean intersections, no self-intersecting garbage
The inference engine, the snapping and axis guessing that makes SketchUp feel like mind reading
3D Warehouse, millions of ready-made components you would otherwise model by hand
The extension ecosystem, which is where half of professional SketchUp workflows actually live
LayOut, DWG and IFC interchange, and anything a contractor or client expects to receive
moatNotes: The inference engine is the product. Everything else is chrome bolted to a geometry kernel nobody wants to rewrite.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a drawing tool is only worth anything if the output survives contact with other people: a fabricator who needs a DWG, a client who needs a dimensioned PDF, a renderer that needs clean manifold geometry. SketchUp is cheap relative to the CAD field and it is the lingua franca for a huge number of small architecture, interiors, and woodworking shops, which means the file format itself is the reason to keep paying. You are not buying push-pull. You are buying the fact that somebody else can open it.
notes: The push-pull demo is a weekend; the kernel is not. The moat is twenty years of geometry edge cases plus a warehouse of models you did not have to build.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user toy 3D modeler in an empty folder. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry, no backend.

Stack, non-negotiable: Vite + TypeScript + three.js. No React. Plain DOM for the toolbar.

Core loop:
1. An orbit-controlled 3D viewport with a ground grid on the XZ plane and basic lighting.
2. Tool: Line. Click points on the ground plane to draw a closed 2D polygon. Snap to grid at 0.1 units, and snap to the first vertex to close the loop. Show a live rubber-band segment.
3. When a loop closes, triangulate it (use three.js ShapeGeometry or an earcut dependency) and add it as a flat face object.
4. Tool: Push-Pull. Click a flat face, drag the mouse to extrude it along its normal, release to commit. Build the extruded solid as an ExtrudeGeometry from the stored 2D outline plus a height. Keep the outline in the object's userData so it can be re-extruded.
5. Tool: Select. Click to select an object, show it highlighted, Delete key removes it.
6. Tool: Move. Drag a selected object along X and Z with grid snapping.

Also required:
- Undo and redo for all operations, via a simple command stack, at least 50 steps deep.
- Export the whole scene to GLTF and to binary STL, both as browser file downloads.
- Save and load the scene as a JSON file containing outlines, heights, and transforms. Do not use localStorage as the only store.
- An on-screen readout of the current tool and the cursor's snapped world coordinates.

Explicitly out of scope, do not attempt: boolean operations, curved surfaces, arcs, textures, materials beyond a single flat color, component instancing, DWG or IFC import, 2D drawing sheets, measurement dimensioning, any kind of multiplayer.

Deliver a README that states plainly which of those limits exist and why. Run npm run build and fix anything that fails before you finish.
